claim: A zonal shift is temporary: you set an initial expiration from one minute up to three days (72 hours), which you can extend, and you can cancel the shift at any time before it expires so that traffic begins returning to the original Availability Zone.
question: How does a zonal shift on a load balancer end, so that traffic returns to the Availability Zone?

values.spoken: three days, which is seventy-two hours

values.display: cancel the shift at any time

qualifiers.scope: per zonal shift on an Application or Network Load Balancer
qualifiers.condition: the expiration is the initial one; you can update the shift to set a new expiration

evidence.quote: All zonal shifts are temporary mitigations. You set an initial expiration when you start a zonal shift, from one minute up to three days (72 hours), which you can extend, if you need to continue the traffic shift.
You can cancel the shift at any time to have traffic begin returning to the original Availability Zone.
You can cancel a zonal shift any time before it expires.

note: requests-14 for fr-0051 (question elb-q019). The ALB start-zonal-shift page also says: All zonal shifts are temporary. You must set an expiration, but you can update active shifts later to set a new expiration.

claim: The Resource Groups Tagging API GetResources operation supports all resource types and returns the tagged or previously tagged resources in the specified Region for the account, and Elastic Load Balancing lets you tag Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, Gateway Load Balancers, target groups, trust stores, listeners, and rules; so a tagged Application Load Balancer, listener, listener rule or target group is a resource type that GetResources supports.
question: Does the Resource Groups Tagging API GetResources operation return tagged Elastic Load Balancing resources (Application Load Balancers, listeners, listener rules and target groups), so that a task can verify its cleanup with a tag filter task=<task id>?

values.display: target groups, trust stores, listeners, and rules

qualifiers.scope: Resource Groups Tagging API GetResources; Elastic Load Balancing resources that carry the tag
qualifiers.condition: the resource carries the tag; GetResources looks only in the Region of the call

evidence.quote: The `GetResources`, `GetTagKeys`, and `GetTagValues` operations support all resource types.
Returns all the tagged or previously tagged resources that are located in the specified AWS Region for the account.

Adds the specified tags to the specified Elastic Load Balancing resource. You can tag your Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers, Gateway Load Balancers, target groups, trust stores, listeners, and rules.

note: requests-14 for fr-0054 (verify steps of elb-t02 and elb-t03). The Tagging API Welcome page lists Elastic Load Balancing among the services that work with the Tagging API (a list item, not quotable); its only GetResources exception named there is IAM users and roles. The Resource Groups supported-resources table lists AWS::ElasticLoadBalancingV2::Listener, ListenerRule, LoadBalancer and TargetGroup as Tag-based Groups: Yes. GetResources is Regional, so the verify call must run in the Region of the task.

claim: An Application Load Balancer listener evaluates its rules in priority order, starting with the lowest numbered rule, and performs the actions of a rule when its conditions are met; when multiple rules match a request, the lower priority number takes precedence, and the actions of the default rule are performed only when the conditions of no other rule are met.
question: When several listener rules of an Application Load Balancer match a request, which rule's actions are performed?

values.display: starting with the lowest numbered rule
the actions for the default rule are performed

evidence.quote: When a listener receives a request, it evaluates the request against each rule in priority order, starting with the lowest numbered rule.

Rules are evaluated in priority order, from the lowest value to the highest value. When the conditions for a rule are met, its actions are performed. If the conditions for no rules are met, the actions for the default rule are performed.

| Priority | The precedence of this rule when multiple rules match. The lower number takes precedence. No two rules can have the same priority.
With a shared load balancer, Elastic Beanstalk treats rule priorities as relative across sharing environments, and maps them to absolute priorities during creation. | `1` | `1` to `1000` |

note: requests-14 for fr-0055 (task elb-t02). The precedence sentence comes from the Elastic Beanstalk namespace aws:elbv2:listenerrule, which defines listener rules for an Application Load Balancer. The Network Load Balancer guide states the same rule for NLB listener rules: If multiple rules match the incoming traffic, the rule with the highest priority (lowest numeric value) takes precedence.
